summaryEn: A Taiwanese skincare brand that became mainland China's largest beauty-salon franchise — about 3,863 of its 4,096 stores are there. It earns an 80% gross margin, holds cash equal to four-fifths of its equity, and pays a 10.5% yield partly out of capital surplus. The store count is shrinking.
model: editorial (truth-audited: FinMind + earnings coverage; franchise framing — the 1989 founding, 1997 China entry, ~80% gross margin, per-store productivity gains and cash-rich balance sheet credited, but the store count's contraction from about 5,033 (c.2021) to 4,096 stated plainly, the NT$10 dividend explained precisely as NT$7 earnings plus NT$3 capital surplus rather than presented as an over-distribution, FY2023's NT$13.05 EPS falling to NT$5.81, non-operating income flagged in FY2025, and weak cash conversion noted; sector Biotech & Healthcare → Beauty Franchise & Skincare; foundedYear set to 1989 with the 2012 Cayman date disclosed)

sections.bodyMarkdown:
Chlitina Holding (麗豐-KY, TWSE: 4137) sells skincare products and services through **beauty salons it does not own**. The **Chlitina brand was founded in Taiwan in 1989 by Dr. Chen Wu-kang**, and in **1997 chairwoman Chen Bi-hua led it into mainland China**, where it became the largest beauty-salon franchise chain in the country. It **listed in Taipei on 27 November 2013** — the first mainland-China beauty chain to do so. *(The Cayman holding company itself was registered in 2012; the founding year shown here is the brand's.)*

The model is franchising. Chlitina recruits and supports franchisees who open salons under its brand, and earns money principally by **selling them skincare products, equipment and training**. That is why the gross margin looks like a software company's — **roughly 80%, running between 79.7% and 83.4%** across recent quarters — and why the operating margin is far lower at **15.5%**: the difference is the cost of recruiting, training, supporting and marketing across thousands of independent stores. As of end-April the network numbered **4,096 stores, of which about 3,863 are in mainland China and 200-plus in Taiwan**.

**The most striking figure is the dividend, and it needs explaining precisely rather than admiring.** Chlitina declared **NT$10 per share against FY2025 EPS of NT$7.13** — which sounds like paying out more than it earns. It is not quite that: the distribution is **NT$7 from earnings plus NT$3 from capital surplus**. The company can do this because it holds **NT$4.38bn of cash against NT$5.58bn of total equity** — roughly **four-fifths of its equity is cash**. At **NT$95.00 that produces a 10.53% yield**, the highest in this collection, on **12.1× earnings and 1.41× book**.

The honest counterweight is the direction of the business. **The store network has contracted** — from roughly **5,033 globally around 2021 to 4,096** now. Earnings fell from **NT$13.05 (FY2023) to NT$5.81 (FY2024)** before recovering to **NT$7.13 (FY2025)**, and FY2025's profit growth came with revenue **down 2%**, achieved through **cost reduction and non-operating income** — 2025Q2 showed a **22.7% net margin against a 15.5% operating margin**. Management has explicitly shifted strategy from opening stores to **raising productivity per store**: average monthly purchases per outlet rose from **RMB 17,000 to RMB 23,000**. **2026Q1 EPS of NT$1.41 doubled** the prior year, though **operating cash flow of NT$52m fell well short of NT$116m of net profit**.

The honest read: **a genuinely profitable, cash-rich brand franchise with an exceptional yield — running a shrinking network in a Chinese consumer market that has been difficult, and distributing capital as well as earnings to maintain the payout.**

Chlitina was founded in **1989 in Taiwan by Dr. Chen Wu-kang**. The name derives from *Christina*, and the founding proposition was **amino-acid-based skincare** delivered not through retail shelves but through **professional beauty salons** — where a trained operator applies the product, explains it, and builds a relationship with a repeat customer.

That channel choice determined everything about the company. Selling skincare through salons means the salon operator is the customer, not the consumer. Chlitina's business therefore became **recruiting, training and supplying franchisees** — providing the brand, the product line, the treatment protocols, the equipment and the marketing, and earning its margin on the products it sells into the network.

In **1997, chairwoman Chen Bi-hua led the group into mainland China**, and the timing was close to ideal. Chinese consumer spending on personal appearance was beginning a multi-decade expansion, the beauty-services industry was almost entirely unbranded and unorganised, and a Taiwanese company arrived with a complete franchise system, a product range and operating know-how. Chlitina expanded across **34 provinces and 380 cities**, and became **mainland China's largest beauty-salon franchise chain**. It **listed in Taipei in November 2013** — the first mainland-China beauty chain to list in Taiwan.

At its peak, around **2021, the network numbered roughly 5,033 stores** worldwide. It now stands at **4,096**, of which about **3,863 are in mainland China**. That contraction is the honest centre of the company's recent history: **Chinese consumer spending weakened, discretionary services suffered, and marginal franchisees closed.**

Management's response has been to stop measuring itself by store count. The stated strategy is now **raising the productivity of each store** — average monthly purchases per outlet have risen from **RMB 17,000 to RMB 23,000** — on the reasoning that a smaller network of stronger operators is worth more than a larger network of weak ones. It is a defensible argument. It is also what a company says when the network is getting smaller.

- **1989** — The **Chlitina** brand is founded in Taiwan by **Dr. Chen Wu-kang**, built on amino-acid skincare sold through professional beauty salons.
- **1997** — Chairwoman **Chen Bi-hua** leads the group into **mainland China**, franchising salons across what becomes 34 provinces and 380 cities.
- **2012** — The **Cayman holding company** is registered.
- **2013 (27 Nov)** — **Lists on the Taiwan Stock Exchange (4137)** — the first mainland-China beauty chain to list in Taiwan.
- **2019** — Dividend of **NT$13.05**, the highest in the recent record.
- **c.2021** — Network reaches roughly **5,033 stores** worldwide, including mainland China, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Vietnam.
- **2022** — **FY2022 EPS NT$8.68**; dividend **NT$7.0**.
- **2023** — **FY2023 EPS NT$13.05** — the peak of the recent record; dividend **NT$10.12**.
- **2024** — **A sharp decline: FY2024 EPS NT$5.81**, down 55%, as Chinese consumer spending weakens; dividend **NT$10.0**.
- **2025** — Revenue falls **2% to NT$3.88bn**, but cost reduction and **non-operating income** lift net profit **over 25% to NT$590m**; **FY2025 EPS NT$7.13**; operating profit **NT$740m**. Dividend of **NT$10.0** declared — **NT$7 from earnings and NT$3 from capital surplus**.
- **2026 (April)** — Network stands at **4,096 stores** (about **3,863** in mainland China, 200-plus in Taiwan). Average monthly purchases per store up from **RMB 17,000** to **RMB 23,000**. **2026Q1 EPS NT$1.41**, double the prior year. Chairman **Chao Cheng-yu** targets double-digit revenue and profit growth for the year.

Chlitina's accounts show **a cash-rich, high-margin franchise business paying out more than its earnings — legitimately, and with a specific mechanism.**

- **Earnings that fell hard and are recovering.** Annual EPS: **NT$8.68 (FY2022) → 13.05 (FY2023) → 5.81 (FY2024) → NT$7.13 (FY2025)**, with **2026Q1 at NT$1.41 against NT$0.68** a year earlier. The **55% fall in FY2024** is the central event, and it tracks Chinese consumer weakness rather than any change in the model.
- **Franchise economics, visible in the margins.** **Gross margin runs 79.7–83.4%** — Chlitina sells products into its network at brand margins. **Operating margin is 15.5%**, and the roughly 65-point gap is the cost of running a franchise system: recruiting, training, supporting and marketing across four thousand independent operators.
- **FY2025's profit growth was not revenue growth.** Revenue **fell 2% to NT$3.88bn** while net profit rose **over 25% to NT$590m**, achieved through **expense reduction and non-operating income**. **2025Q2 showed a 22.7% net margin against a 15.5% operating margin** — a substantial non-operating contribution. Operating profit for the year was **NT$740m**.
- **The dividend, explained exactly.** The **NT$10.0 declared for FY2025 against EPS of NT$7.13** is **NT$7 from earnings and NT$3 from capital surplus**. This is not an unsustainable over-distribution of profit; it is a deliberate return of capital by a company that holds **NT$4.38bn of cash against NT$5.58bn of total equity** — roughly **79% of equity in cash**. The **10.53% yield** at NT$95.00 is real, and part of it is the company handing back its own balance sheet.
- **Cash conversion is weak.** **2026Q1 operating cash flow of NT$52m** against **NT$116m of net income**. For a business with 80% gross margins this deserves watching — franchise receivables and inventory in the network can absorb cash.
- **A long record of large distributions.** Cash dividends (FinMind, by fiscal year): **NT$12.0 (2018) → 13.05 (2019) → 8.5 → 12.0 (2021) → 7.0 (2022) → 10.12 (2023) → 10.0 (2024) → NT$10.0 (2025)**.
- **A conservative balance sheet.** **NT$9.82bn of assets** on **NT$5.58bn of equity**, a **43.2% debt ratio**, and **trailing return on equity of 11.63%**. Valuation is **12.1× earnings and 1.41× book**.

The financing reality: **a cash-heavy franchise generating high margins on a contracting network, returning both profits and capital while it works on making each remaining store worth more.**

**Stance: mainland China's largest beauty-salon franchise, earning 80% gross margins with four-fifths of its equity in cash and paying a 10.53% yield — on a network that has shrunk from about 5,033 stores to 4,096.**

The bull case:

1. **A genuinely branded position in a fragmented industry.** **4,096 stores**, about **3,863 in mainland China**, built since **1997** across 34 provinces and 380 cities — in a beauty-services market that remains largely unbranded and unorganised. That is a real asset and slow to replicate.
2. **Franchise economics.** **Gross margin of roughly 80%** because Chlitina sells products and systems rather than operating salons itself. Capital intensity sits with the franchisees, not the company.
3. **A balance sheet that funds the yield.** **NT$4.38bn of cash against NT$5.58bn of equity** and a **43.2% debt ratio**. The **NT$10 dividend** — **NT$7 from earnings, NT$3 from capital surplus** — is affordable precisely because of that cash, giving a **10.53% yield** at **12.1× earnings**.
4. **The productivity strategy is working, so far.** Average monthly purchases per store up from **RMB 17,000 to RMB 23,000**, and **2026Q1 EPS doubled** to NT$1.41. Management guides double-digit revenue and profit growth for 2026.

The counter-arguments:

- **The network is contracting.** From roughly **5,033 stores around 2021 to 4,096** — about a fifth smaller. Franchise businesses are valued on network growth, and this one is going the other way.
- **Earnings are well below the peak.** **NT$13.05 (FY2023) → NT$5.81 (FY2024) → NT$7.13 (FY2025)**.
- **FY2025's profit rise came with falling revenue**, helped by **cost cuts and non-operating income** — not by the business growing.
- **This is a bet on Chinese discretionary consumer spending**, which has been weak, in a services category consumers can postpone.
- **Cash conversion is soft** — **NT$52m of operating cash flow against NT$116m of net profit** in 2026Q1.

A **cash-return** thesis: an unusually profitable franchise with a genuine brand, paying out heavily while it stabilises — where the yield is the return and the network trend is the risk.

Chlitina makes money by **supplying an army of salons it does not own**:

- **The franchise structure.** Independent operators open beauty salons under the **Chlitina** brand. Chlitina provides the brand, the product range, treatment protocols, equipment, training and marketing support. The franchisee provides the premises, the staff and the capital.
- **Where the revenue actually comes from.** Principally **selling skincare products and supplies into the network**. Each of the **4,096 stores** buys product continuously to serve its customers — currently averaging about **RMB 23,000 per store per month**, up from RMB 17,000. That is why the metric management now emphasises is **purchases per store**, not store count: **revenue is store count multiplied by store productivity**, and if the first is falling, the second must rise faster.
- **Why the gross margin is roughly 80%.** Chlitina sells branded, formulated skincare at brand margins into its own franchise channel. It does not bear the salon's rent, staff or equipment costs — those sit with the franchisee. **The company's costs are the franchise system itself**: recruitment, training, field support, marketing and product development, which is why the **operating margin is 15.5%** rather than 80%.
- **Geographic concentration.** About **3,863 of 4,096 stores are in mainland China**, with 200-plus in Taiwan and a presence in Hong Kong and Vietnam. **This is, financially, a Chinese consumer business with a Taiwanese listing.**
- **The capital position.** **NT$4.38bn of cash against NT$5.58bn of equity.** The model requires little capital — franchisees fund the stores — so cash accumulates, which is why the company can distribute **NT$3 per share from capital surplus** on top of earnings.

The levers are **store count, purchases per store, product mix and Chinese consumer confidence**. The strength is a capital-light, high-margin brand position in a fragmented market, funded entirely from cash. The vulnerability is structural to franchising: **Chlitina's revenue depends on the health of thousands of small independent businesses it does not control** — and when their customers cut back, franchisees close, which is exactly what took the network from about 5,033 to 4,096.

China's beauty-services industry is enormous, fragmented, and difficult to consolidate.

- **The market's shape.** Beauty and skincare services in mainland China are delivered overwhelmingly by **small, independent, unbranded salons**. That fragmentation is the opportunity a franchise system exists to address: a branded network offers consumers consistency and offers operators products, training and marketing they could not develop alone. **Chlitina became the largest such chain** by starting early — in **1997** — and building through 34 provinces and 380 cities.
- **Why franchising rather than ownership.** Beauty salons are local, labour-intensive and management-dependent. Operating thousands directly would require enormous capital and a management structure to match. Franchising pushes that to the operator and lets the brand owner scale on **product supply and systems** — which is why Chlitina earns **80% gross margins with a 43.2% debt ratio and no store-level capital**.
- **The cyclical exposure.** Beauty services are **discretionary and deferrable**. When Chinese consumer confidence weakened, treatment frequency fell, salon revenue fell, and the weakest franchisees closed. The network contraction **from about 5,033 to 4,096** is that process, and it is the industry's characteristic risk rather than a company-specific failure.
- **Competition.** Domestic Chinese beauty chains, international skincare brands selling through retail and e-commerce, and — increasingly — **medical aesthetics**, which has drawn spending toward injectables and device-based treatments and away from traditional salon services. Chinese e-commerce also gives consumers direct access to skincare products that salons once supplied.
- **What the collection shows about this exposure.** Several companies profiled here depend on Chinese consumer demand — **Gourmet Master (2723)** in restaurants, **Airtac (1590)** in factory equipment. All have found the same thing: the Chinese market's scale is real, and so is its volatility.

Chlitina's position is **the strongest available in a structurally fragmented industry** — but franchising converts consumer weakness into store closures with a lag, and the company's revenue follows. The industry truth is that **a franchise network is only as strong as its weakest franchisees' economics**, and those are set by consumers, not by the brand.

**Strengths**
- **Mainland China's largest beauty-salon franchise**: **4,096 stores**, about **3,863** in China, built since 1997 across 34 provinces and 380 cities.
- **Franchise economics**: gross margin around **80%**, capital-light, **43.2% debt ratio**.
- **Cash of NT$4.38bn against NT$5.58bn of equity** — roughly **79% of equity in cash**.
- **10.53% dividend yield** at **12.1× earnings**, funded as **NT$7 from earnings plus NT$3 from capital surplus**.

**Weaknesses**
- **Network contracting**: from roughly **5,033 stores (c.2021) to 4,096**.
- **Earnings well below peak**: **NT$13.05 (FY2023) → NT$5.81 (FY2024) → NT$7.13 (FY2025)**.
- **FY2025 profit growth came with revenue down 2%**, aided by cost cuts and **non-operating income**.
- **Weak cash conversion**: **NT$52m operating cash flow** against **NT$116m** of 2026Q1 net profit.

**Opportunities**
- **Per-store productivity** rising — RMB 17,000 to RMB 23,000 monthly purchases.
- Management guidance for **double-digit revenue and profit growth** in 2026; **2026Q1 EPS doubled**.
- Consolidation of an unbranded industry if Chinese consumer confidence recovers.

**Threats**
- **Chinese discretionary consumer weakness** closing more franchised stores.
- **Medical aesthetics** drawing spending away from traditional salon services.
- E-commerce disintermediating salon-channel skincare sales.

- **The network is shrinking (the central risk).** From roughly **5,033 stores around 2021 to 4,096** — about a fifth smaller. A franchise business earns from the number of outlets buying its products; a contracting network is a contracting revenue base unless per-store productivity rises faster, which is precisely why management has changed the metric it emphasises.
- **Chinese discretionary consumer demand.** About **3,863 of 4,096 stores are in mainland China**, and beauty services are among the easiest expenditures for a consumer to postpone. **FY2024's 55% earnings collapse** followed exactly that.
- **The dividend includes a return of capital.** The **NT$10.0** payment is **NT$7 from earnings and NT$3 from capital surplus**. That is legitimate and well funded — **NT$4.38bn of cash against NT$5.58bn of equity** — but the capital-surplus component is finite, and the **10.53% yield** is not entirely a yield on earnings.
- **Profit improvement without revenue improvement.** FY2025's **25%+ net profit growth** came with revenue **down 2%**, via **cost reduction and non-operating income** (2025Q2's net margin of 22.7% against a 15.5% operating margin). Cost reduction has a floor; non-operating income does not repeat reliably.
- **Cash conversion.** **NT$52m of operating cash flow against NT$116m of net profit** in 2026Q1. In a business with 80% gross margins, profit should convert to cash readily; when it does not, receivables and channel inventory are the usual explanation.
- **Franchisee dependence.** Chlitina does not control its stores' rent, staffing or local management. Its revenue is the aggregate health of thousands of small independent businesses.

Chlitina's outlook depends on **whether per-store productivity can outrun the shrinking store count.** The axes to watch:

- **Store count.** **4,096 as of April**, from about **5,033 around 2021**. Stabilisation would be the clearest sign that Chinese consumer conditions have bottomed; further contraction means the productivity gains are running against a widening headwind.
- **Purchases per store.** Up from **RMB 17,000 to RMB 23,000** a month. This is management's chosen metric and the direct multiplier on revenue — **revenue is store count times store productivity**, and only one of those is currently rising.
- **Revenue growth, not just profit growth.** FY2025's profit rose while revenue **fell 2%**, on cost cuts and non-operating income. Management guides **double-digit revenue and profit growth** for 2026, and **2026Q1 EPS doubled to NT$1.41** — revenue is the honest test of whether that is happening.
- **Cash conversion.** **NT$52m of operating cash flow against NT$116m of net profit** in 2026Q1. For an 80%-gross-margin franchise, this should be considerably better.
- **The composition of the dividend.** **NT$7 from earnings, NT$3 from capital surplus.** Whether future payments rely less on capital surplus indicates whether earnings are genuinely recovering.

Bottom line: Chlitina built **mainland China's largest beauty-salon franchise** from a Taiwanese skincare brand founded in **1989**, and earns **roughly 80% gross margins** doing it, with **four-fifths of its equity in cash** and a **10.53% yield** — of which **NT$3 of the NT$10 is a return of capital**. It is also running a network that has **shrunk from about 5,033 stores to 4,096**, earnings **well below the FY2023 peak**, and FY2025 profit growth achieved on **falling revenue**. Judge it on **store count and revenue** — a genuinely profitable brand, paying you well while it tries to stop getting smaller.
